d.title: One ratio separates the two worlds, and both runs took about eight seconds
d.caption: **`cpu/wall` is the whole diagnostic: 2% means the process spent eight seconds waiting and a fifth of a second computing; 98% means it was busy the entire time.** Both finished in roughly the same wall-clock, **so the duration tells you nothing about which strategy will help** — threads will fix the first and do nothing for the second. Which is why this is the first measurement in the module: **it is two lines of `time.process_time()` against `time.perf_counter()`, and it decides the whole chapter.**

d.title: A daemon thread does not run its `finally` blocks
d.caption: **That is the row that matters and the one the name does not suggest: a daemon thread is killed abruptly at interpreter exit, so cleanup is skipped — files unclosed, buffers unflushed.** Which makes the choice concrete rather than stylistic: **anything holding a resource should not be a daemon, however much you want the process to exit promptly.** And the non-daemon risk is the mirror image: **a hung thread blocks exit forever**, so the real answer for background work is usually **a non-daemon thread plus a shutdown event it checks.**

d.title: `maxsize` is the important argument, and the default is unbounded
d.caption: **An unbounded queue lets a fast producer read the entire input into memory while the consumers fall behind** — so the queue that was supposed to decouple them becomes the place the whole dataset lives. `maxsize` makes `put()` block, **which is backpressure: the producer is slowed to the rate the consumers can sustain, for free and with no extra code.** And the structural argument over a lock: **a queue hands ownership across rather than sharing it, so there is no window in which two threads can both see the same object** — 2.5's bug, designed out.

nodes.label: A fast producer reads everything in
And a queue hands ownership across

d.title: Shared memory was seven times faster than pickling 400 MB per worker
d.caption: **~6.4 s to pickle 400 MB per worker against ~0.9 s with `shared_memory` — because the second copies nothing.** The rows to avoid are the last two in a different way each: **`Manager().dict()` is very slow, since every single access is a round trip to a server process**, so a loop reading it is a loop making IPC calls. And the honest note on the fast path: **shared memory is zero-copy and you manage the lifetime**, so a crashed worker can leave a segment behind that nothing will clean up.

d.title: A worker's exception is printed to stderr and lost, or re-raised on `.result()`
d.caption: **The first row is the whole reason this layer exists: a raw thread that raises prints to stderr and the caller never knows** — so a batch of twenty tasks can lose three and report success. `concurrent.futures` re-raises on `.result()`, **which turns a silent partial failure into an exception at the point you asked for the answer.** And the row that pays off later: **switching between threads and processes is one class name**, so the experiment 11.1 implies costs a one-word edit rather than a rewrite.

state: a shared list or a queue

d.title: A timeout bounds your waiting, not the work
d.caption: **The worker keeps running, keeps holding its thread, and keeps whatever resource it acquired** — so a `timeout=` on `.result()` lets *you* move on and changes nothing about the task. Which is the thing to internalise: **you cannot cancel a running task.** `future.cancel()` succeeds only while the task is still queued, **so a pool whose workers are all busy will return `False` for every cancel you attempt**, and a shutdown that waits for them is the only honest option — or `shutdown(cancel_futures=True)` for the ones that never started.

nodes.label: So a busy pool cancels nothing
shutdown(cancel_futures=True)
nodes.sub: for the ones not yet started

d.title: Calling an async function returns a coroutine object and runs none of it
d.caption: **`fetch(url)` without `await` gives you `<coroutine object fetch at 0x...>` — which is the most common `asyncio` bug, and it produces a warning rather than an error, so it survives code review.** The second confusion is as costly and harder to see: **`await` in a loop is sequential — awaiting a hundred fetches one after another takes as long as doing them serially**, because `await` means *wait here*, not *start this*. **Concurrency comes from `gather` or a task group**, and that is the third distinction: **a coroutine is a recipe, a task is a scheduled one.**

steps.code: for u in urls: await fetch(u)
await gather(*(fetch(u) for u in urls))

state: scheduled - it runs without an await

d.title: Five bridges, and `asyncio.run` inside a running loop raises
d.caption: **`asyncio.run` creates and closes a loop, so calling it from inside a coroutine is the error `asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop`** — use it once, at the entry point. The workhorse is the second row: **`await asyncio.to_thread(fn)` is one line around a legacy blocking call you cannot replace.** And the third is the distinction people get wrong: **CPU-bound work needs a *process* pool, because pure Python in a thread contends for the GIL** — so `to_thread` on a tight numeric loop buys nothing.

d.title: Seven symptoms, and each one has a one-command check
d.caption: **“Threads made it slower” is GIL contention and the check is `cpu/wall` from 11.1** — which is why that measurement comes first. Two are easy to miss: **fast locally and slow on a bigger machine is nested library parallelism, fixed with `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1`**, because NumPy's threads multiply by your workers rather than dividing the work. And **“works, then 429s from upstream” is a concurrency limit with no rate limit** — bounding how many run at once says nothing about how fast they start.
